definition: A shared communication link consisting of a set of wires that connects multiple components in a digital system.
A set of rules governing the exchange of data over a bus, defining signal timings, states, and sequences.
The routing logic (muxes, crossbars, bridges) that connects multiple masters and slaves, acting as the physical implementation of the bus architecture.
A direct connection between exactly one master and one slave without shared bus wires.
A complete operation on a bus, typically consisting of an address phase followed by one or more data phases.
A single data transfer within a transaction. A burst consists of multiple beats.
A type of transaction where a single address phase is followed by multiple data beats, improving throughput.
A signal convention where the logical 'true' or 'active' state is represented by a low voltage level (0). Often denoted with an 'n' suffix (e.g., RESETn).
The period of time during which a signal's value is stable and guaranteed to be sampled correctly by the receiving logic.
The ability of a receiving entity (slave) to stall the sending entity (master) when it is not ready to accept data, typically using a READY signal.
A signaling mechanism used to coordinate data transfer between two components, ensuring both are ready. Examples include Request/Grant and Ready/Valid.
A capability where transactions can complete in a different order than they were issued, based on IDs or tags, to prevent stalling on slow slaves.
A state where two or more operations are each waiting for the other to finish, resulting in the system freezing indefinitely.
A state where components continuously change state in response to each other without making any forward progress.
